prompt: Tell Miko the food is good.
why: *Olleya oota* is “good food”: it names the food but doesn't say anything about it. To say the food IS good, put *oota* first and end with {answer}.
note: The trigger case. Drill-level so it beats the vocab line below on an exact "olleya oota".

why: *Olleya* is “good” before a thing, as in *olleya oota*. It can't end a sentence. To say something IS good, end with {answer}.
note: Covers "oota olleya" and later drills (L16 "Oota tumba chennagide").

why: *Oota chennagide* is a whole sentence, “the food is good”. For just “good food”, the good word goes first: {answer} *oota*.
*Chennagide* is “it is good”, a whole sentence on its own. Right before a thing, “good” is {answer}.
*Chennagiddeeni* is “I am fine”, about yourself. For a thing, the end is *ide*, “it is”: {answer}.
note: Likelihood medium: same stem, L9 teach links them.

why: *Chennagide* is “it is good”, about a thing. About yourself, “I am fine” is {answer}.
note: Fires only in review after L9.

why: *Pustakagalu* is “books”, more than one. *Idu* points at one thing, so it's one book: {answer}.
note: Drill-level, not on the Pustaka word: a vocab trap would also fire on L7 "Eradu pustaka", where "pustakagalu" is good Kannada (see report).

why: *Pustakagalu* is “books”, more than one. *Idu* points at one thing, so it's one book: {answer}.
note: Fires in review after L8. Matches both L2 drills with this answer.

prompt: Ask how much the book is.
why: *Pustakagalu* is “books”, more than one. This asks about one book: {answer}.
*Pustaka* is one book. For more than one, add -galu: {answer}.
*Hoovu* is one flower. For more than one, add -galu: {answer}.
*Mane* is one house. For more than one, add -galu: {answer}.
*Snehita* is one friend. Friends are people, so for more than one add -aru, not -galu: {answer}.
note: Snehitagalu itself cannot carry a trap (untaught words are skipped); the grammarNote covers it.

why: *Beda* is “don't want”. To say you want it, use {answer} in its place.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Beku* is “want”. To say you don't want it, use {answer} in its place.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Oota illa* is “there's no food”. To turn food down, use the don't-want word: {answer}.
*Neevu* is “you”. “Water” sounds close but ends in -ru: {answer}.
note: Sound-alike slip; likelihood low-medium.

why: *Illi* is “here”. “No” ends in -a: {answer}.
*Illa* is “no”. “Here” ends in -i: {answer}.
note: Fires after L4.

why: *Adu* is “that”, something far off. For something near you, it's {answer}.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Idu* is “this”, something near you. For something far off, it's {answer}.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Alli* is “there”, far off. For “here”, near you, it's {answer}.
*Illi* is “here”, near you. For “there”, far off, it's {answer}.
*Ide* is “there is”, saying a thing is somewhere. For the place “there”, it's {answer}.
note: Keep it after the Illi trap in the array: "Mane alli ide" contains ide, so the exact match fires on any miss there until the guard lands.

why: *Mane alli* is just “house there”. To say the house IS there, end with {answer}.
*Alli* is “there”. To ask “where?”, it's {answer}.
note: Likelihood medium: same -lli.

why: *Hogu* is “go!”, telling someone else to go. For yourself, “I go”, it's {answer}.
note: Hogu has alt "hogi", so a learner typing hogi also gets this; still true.

why: *Hoguttene* is “I go”, about yourself. To tell someone to go, it's {answer}.
note: Drill-level, not on the Hogu word: Hogu carries alt "hogi", so a vocab trap would fire on L14 "Hogi baruttene", where hogi means "having gone".

why: *Naanu* is “I”. Before a thing, “my” is {answer}.
*Neevu* is “you”. Before a thing, “your” is {answer}.
*Nanna* is “my”, your own. For the person you're talking to, “your” is {answer}.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Nimma* is “your”, the person you're talking to. For your own, “my” is {answer}.
note: Needs the exact-match guard (see report): later drills contain both words, e.g. L15+ "Nanage idu beku, aadare adu beda".

why: *Aatana* is a plain “his”, for a man. For “her”, or anyone you respect, it's {answer}.
*Avaru* is “that person”, over there. For the person right here, start with i-: {answer}.
*Ivaru* is “this person”, right here. For someone over there, start with a-: {answer}.
*Idu* is “this” for a thing. For a person, it's {answer}, “this person”, and it's polite too.
*Adu* is “that” for a thing. For a person, it's {answer}, “that person”, and it's polite too.
*Yenu* is “what”, for things. For a person, “who” is {answer}.
*Yaaru* is “who”, for people. For a thing, “what” is {answer}.

why: *Hege* is “how”, as in *hegiddeera?*. For a price or an amount, “how much”, it's {answer}.
*Ide* is “it is”, for things. For yourself, “I am” is {answer}.
note: Will not fire on L11/L12 drills while "naanu illi ide" is accepted (see report).

why: *Hogu* is “go!”, telling someone else to go. For “I am going” right now, it's {answer}.
*Ninne* is “yesterday”, behind you. For “tomorrow”, ahead of you, it's {answer}.
*Naale* is “tomorrow”, ahead of you. For “yesterday”, behind you, it's {answer}.
*Naalku* is the number four. “Tomorrow” is {answer}.

why: *Eega* is “now”, this moment. For the whole day, “today”, it's {answer}.
note: Likelihood medium. Accuracy is solid; medium only because "eega" and "ivattu" overlap in some English prompts ("today I am working" vs "I am working now").

why: *Ivattu* is “today”, the whole day. For “now”, this moment, it's {answer}.
note: Fires after L12. Same caveat.

why: *Hoguttene* is “I go” or “I will go”. For “I went”, the word changes: {answer}.
*Hoguttiddene* is “I am going”, right now. For “I went”, the word changes: {answer}.
*Maaduttiddene* is “I am doing”, right now. For “I did”, it's {answer}.
*Tinnuttiddene* is “I am eating”, right now. For “I ate”, it's {answer}.
*Manege* is “to the house”, for going there. You saw the house itself, so it's plain {answer}.
